taches.questions:
Accurate time series forecasting is critically important for numerous applications, including traffic management and disease control, and the field has attracted significant research attention in recent years. A major challenge is the frequent occurrence of distribution shift in time series data: the patterns in the data change over time, so the data encountered during deployment differ from those a model was trained on. In traffic flow prediction, for instance, vehicle counts at an intersection are influenced by factors such as public preference for private vehicles, temperature or economic conditions; if the economy is prosperous during the training period but declines during deployment, people may become less willing to drive and traffic volumes fall. Furthermore, since data arrive sequentially once a model is deployed, adjusting a pre-trained forecasting model to make online predictions is a particularly important problem.

In existing research, online time series prediction proceeds as a repeating loop: the model is first updated with newly acquired data and then deployed at the next time step; when new data arrive at that step, the model is updated again and applied to the following step. The fundamental method within this framework is online gradient descent (OGD): upon observing a sample, the loss is computed, the model's parameters are immediately updated, and the updated model is used at the next time step. Most existing online time series learning methods can be regarded as enhancements or variations of this procedure, so the core challenges they address come down to two questions: which parameters to update, and how to update them.

Regarding which parameters to update, most methods avoid updating all of the model's parameters, because updating an entire deep model from single observations is unstable. Some update only the parameters of the final prediction layer; others update the ensemble weights that combine several models, the weights of convolutional layers, or low-rank scaling coefficients of the model weights. Many methods keep the base model frozen and update only a small adapter module, typically a few simple multilayer perceptrons with few parameters, placed after the model's output or on both its input and its output; the reduced number of adjusted parameters yields more stable updates. Regarding how the updates are performed, gradients estimated from a single sample have high variance, and many methods refine the basic scheme: they use a small batch of recent samples, add previously seen samples through experience replay or select similar samples from a stored memory, combine a fast stream updated with gradients from recent samples and a slow stream updated with gradients aggregated over many past samples, update only when a distribution drift is detected, or bypass gradients altogether by directly fitting the parameters of a linear adapter on a small batch of samples. Aggregating more samples reduces the variance of the gradient estimate but can bias it with outdated information. Theoretical work on online optimization makes this tension explicit: the dynamic regret of online gradient descent grows with the cumulative variation of the optimal parameters over time and, when gradients are estimated from samples rather than from the expected loss, with the variance of these estimates.

A separate line of work addresses distribution shift through normalization, computing normalization statistics individually for each sample, forecasting future statistics from past ones, or using more informative statistics, so that the data fed to the model at each time step follow a more standardized distribution. These strategies primarily target covariate shift, in which the distribution of the input changes while the relationship from input to target remains the same; they are ineffective against concept drift, in which that relationship itself changes.

The core challenge of online time series forecasting therefore lies in identifying appropriate parameters and devising effective update strategies. This raises a question that existing work has largely taken for granted: are the parameters typically chosen for updating, such as final-layer weights or adapters attached to a model's input or output, truly the best quantities to adapt in a pre-trained forecaster when the conditions that generate the data change?

A second difficulty concerns how updates can be made in multi-step forecasting. When a model forecasts the next H steps, the true values for a forecast made at time t are not all available until time t+H, so the error, and consequently the gradient, that can be computed at time t must rely on the forecast made H steps earlier. This delayed feedback introduces a potentially harmful lag and can make gradient-based updates unreliable, on top of the high variance of gradients estimated from few samples. How should a pre-trained deep forecasting model be adapted online so that it keeps up with evolving patterns, including concept drift, despite delayed and noisy feedback, and which components of the model should such adaptation target?

taches.questions:
Semantic segmentation has improved significantly with recent advances in deep neural networks, but it requires a large volume of fine-grained pixel-level labels, which are time-consuming and labor-intensive to obtain. Because images themselves are readily available, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) and semi-supervised learning (SSL) have been introduced to handle label-scarce scenarios: UDA learns from labeled synthetic data and transfers knowledge to real, unlabeled target domains, while SSL uses a tiny portion of annotated data to generalize to unseen data. Both are gaining attention as promising ways to reduce the reliance on extensive annotation in semantic segmentation.

In both settings, models are trained on annotated and unlabeled data simultaneously. Mainstream methods follow two paradigms. Self-training methods use a temporally smoothed exponential moving average (EMA) model as a teacher to generate stable pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, while consistency regularization methods encourage the model to produce consistent predictions for the same sample under different perturbation views; recent state-of-the-art methods combine the two. Both can be summarized as pseudo-label learning, in which the network's own predictions serve as supervision for unlabeled data. In the widely adopted form of this paradigm, the teacher's prediction is converted into a hard pseudo-label through an argmax and encoded one-hot, a confidence-based quality estimate (threshold filtering or a weighting function) controls how much each pseudo-label contributes, and training uses a cross-entropy loss.

Despite promising results, pseudo-labels inevitably contain errors that mislead training, and these errors are further amplified during training because of the one-hot encoding. Typical remedies use filter-out mechanisms that train only on high-confidence pseudo-labels, but this makes the model focus on easy samples while neglecting difficult ones, resulting in sub-optimal performance. Another alternative assigns weights according to pseudo-label confidence, but such weighting functions require careful design and selection of hyperparameters, which compromises their applicability. Other work designs new optimization criteria, for example inspired by negative learning. Existing work thus concentrates on selection strategies for pseudo-labels and rarely considers the impact of the encoding form assigned to classes.

This omission matters most for confusing classes. For instance, pixels of the class sheep may be confused by the classifier with horse or cow, and the resulting erroneous pseudo-label is encoded one-hot through the argmax, committing the supervision entirely to a wrong class. Similar classes plausibly share common visual attributes (sheep and cows, for example, both have horns and hooves), which leads to confusing pseudo-labels that further misguide training, yet a one-hot target cannot express what the confused classes have in common. How to utilize the shared attributes among confusing classes to design a suitable encoding form for pseudo-label learning remains rarely explored.

This raises several questions. Can the class encoding used by the segmentation model and its pseudo-labels be redesigned so that supervision stays informative even when the class decision for a pixel is wrong? Under such an encoding, how should pseudo-labels be generated from the teacher's predictions so that they introduce less noise than hard one-hot labels, and what training objective is appropriate? Can an alternative encoding be shown, both theoretically and empirically, to match one-hot encoding in the fully supervised setting while being more robust to label noise in pseudo-label learning? Finally, since the encoding form is orthogonal to pseudo-label selection strategies, can such a change be integrated into existing self-training and consistency-regularization frameworks for both UDA and SSL, across different segmentation architectures?

taches.questions:
Modern generative paradigms, including diffusion, flow matching and consistency models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance and form the backbone of leading image and video generation systems, including large multi-modal generative models. Despite their success, they share a critical drawback: both training and sampling demand substantial computational resources. Multi-step frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching produce a sample by iteratively integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, typically requiring 40 to 100 network function evaluations (NFEs). The problem is magnified for large-scale models, for which efficient sampling is paramount: the continuous, long-term cost of inference often surpasses the one-time training cost, directly affecting economic viability and practical deployment. For example, the largest open multi-modal image generators (about 20B parameters) typically need about 100 NFEs, i.e. roughly 40 seconds on a single A100 GPU for one 1024×1024 image.

Numerous efforts aim to accelerate generative inference by reducing the number of sampling steps. Early single-step generators such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffered from unstable training dynamics. To accelerate multi-step diffusion models, various distillation techniques have been introduced. They range from student-teacher methods, in which a student learns to reproduce a frozen teacher's sampling trajectory in fewer steps (e.g., progressive distillation, which requires an iterative distillation procedure), to distribution matching distillation (e.g., DMD and DMD2), which uses adversarial-style training with auxiliary networks to align the generator's output distribution directly with the data distribution. In parallel, consistency models and their variants (e.g., LCM and PCM), as well as related shortcut and MeanFlow objectives, have been designed explicitly for high-quality generation in very few steps, and recent work shows that multi-step and few-step models can be cast as instances of a single unified any-step training objective.

Despite this progress, existing few-step methods face a difficult trade-off between simplicity, efficiency and quality. (a) Complexity and instability: adversarial approaches, such as GANs, DMD-style distribution matching and hybrid frameworks that combine teacher guidance with adversarial signals (e.g., SANA-Sprint), require auxiliary trained networks (discriminators or fake-sample score networks) and/or frozen teacher models; distribution matching methods typically keep separate copies of a generator, a real-score model and a fake-score model. This introduces training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters, and it increases architectural complexity and GPU memory overhead. For ultra-large models, the added complexity often translates into out-of-memory failures or brittle training dynamics, so few-step approaches have rarely been applied to models beyond about 3B parameters, and the only open-source few-step model released for a large model was obtained by distribution matching distillation with its GAN loss removed, an indirect sign of the high cost of adversarial losses at scale. (b) Performance degradation: methods trained without adversarial guidance, such as consistency models, often show a sharp decline in quality at very low NFEs (fewer than 4), and within the unified any-step view, current few-step methods struggle to reach high-quality one-step generation without resorting to a GAN-style loss.

The open problem is therefore how to train a generator that produces high-quality images in a single function evaluation, or very few, without discriminators, auxiliary score networks or frozen teacher models, so that training remains simple, stable and memory-efficient enough to scale to full-parameter training of the largest (10B to 20B parameters) text-to-image and multi-modal generators, without sacrificing the quality obtained by multi-step sampling.

taches.questions:
Modern text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models generate images of unprecedented diversity and quality from natural-language descriptions, and progress in architectures and theoretical foundations has allowed them to scale to billions of parameters. This paradigm works well for concise prompts but falters when the input becomes a descriptive paragraph. While a model may excel at rendering "a house in the middle of a forest", it often fails when the prompt expands, detailing the terracotta roof tiles, the weathered white panels of the house, and the striking contrast cast by the afternoon sun.

This failure stems from a fundamental conflict between the nature of long-form text and the models' training paradigm. T2I models are predominantly trained on vast datasets of images paired with short, concise, often label-like captions. They learn to map keywords and short phrases to visual features, but are undertrained on interpreting the narrative flow and distributed details of a paragraph, so a descriptive paragraph is effectively an out-of-distribution input for them. Part of the difficulty is often attributed to the fixed context window of text encoders such as CLIP, which can be lifted by switching to more powerful language models; yet even modern models that use powerful text encoders struggle on these inputs, missing more than half of the specified objects.

Existing methods attempt to bridge this gap through two strategies. The most direct approach fine-tunes the T2I model on long-captioned data. While effective within the training lengths, it requires intensive tuning, extrapolating to even longer prompts remains challenging, and the tuned models risk "catastrophic forgetting" of their pre-trained knowledge. The second strategy adopts projection-based methods that map the long prompt, typically encoded by a language model, into the effective context window or original text-embedding space of the pre-trained model. There, the information bottleneck sacrifices the very details that make long prompts compelling.

These limitations reveal an open question: how can we utilize a pre-trained model's existing knowledge of short prompts to render long, intricate paragraphs, preserving their many details while remaining robust as prompts grow longer than those seen during training?

taches.questions:
Smoothed decision-making is critical to avoiding abrupt and potentially dangerous large changes of actions in many online optimization problems, such as energy production scheduling in power grids, object tracking, motion planning, and server capacity provisioning in data centers. Mathematically, action smoothness can be achieved by adding to the optimization objective a switching cost that penalizes temporal changes in actions. The switching cost equips the online objective with a (finite) memory of previous actions and creates substantial algorithmic challenges; smoothed online optimization has therefore received a great deal of attention over the last decade, with a quickly growing list of algorithms offering worst-case performance guarantees in adversarial and stochastic settings and under various extensions.

At the same time, long-term fairness is a crucial consideration in many online optimization problems that can profoundly affect individuals' well-being and social welfare. Sequential allocation of social goods to different individuals or groups must be fair and free of discrimination; the surging environmental costs of geographically distributed AI data centers must be fairly distributed across regions, as repeatedly called for by various organizations and government agencies; and AI model performance and resource provisioning must promote social fairness without adversely affecting disadvantaged individuals or groups. If not designed with fairness in mind, online algorithms can perpetuate or even exacerbate societal biases, disproportionately affect certain groups or individuals, and amplify already widening socioeconomic disparities. Fairness in online optimization is therefore not only an ethical concern but also a necessity for broader social responsibility.

Incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into the objective can effectively promote fairness in online optimization by mitigating implicit or explicit biases, but it creates significant challenges. The regularizer depends on the entire trajectory of actions and contexts and can only be evaluated at the end of an episode, with complete information, whereas a switching cost can be assessed step by step. Online decision-makers react to sequentially revealed information and tend to prioritize immediate cost reduction, potentially neglecting the long-term consequences of their sequence of decisions.

Recent research has started to explore fairness and long-term constraints in online problems such as online resource allocation, using primal-dual techniques. A major limitation of current fair online algorithms, however, is their reliance on the assumption that per-round objective functions are independent of historical actions, an assumption that plays a pivotal role in both their algorithm design and their theoretical analysis. In a simple resource allocation problem, for instance, the maximum allowable action at a given time may depend on past decisions through the remaining budget, but the reward at that time is assumed to depend only on the current decision. Such methods fall short when the per-round objective is directly affected by previous irrevocable actions, as it is with switching costs; in that case an online algorithm and an offline benchmark face different per-round objectives because their action sequences differ, which complicates any direct comparison of their costs. Conversely, the rich literature on smoothed online optimization does not handle a regularizer that is evaluated over the whole horizon. Fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs is thus a new and challenging setting that appears not to have been considered in the literature.

Formally, consider an episode of T rounds. At each round t, an agent observes a (potentially adversarially chosen) non-negative hitting cost function f_t and a matrix A_t that maps its action into an M-dimensional cost vector, each dimension corresponding to an entity for which fairness must be taken into account, and then chooses an irrevocable action x_t without knowing future information. It incurs the hitting cost f_t(x_t) and a switching cost d(x_t, x_{t-1}), for instance a scaled squared Euclidean distance between consecutive actions. Fairness is captured by a long-term cost g, convex and Lipschitz, applied to the episode average of the cost vectors; a well-known choice is an l_p norm, which prioritizes reducing the highest costs borne by disadvantaged entities and recovers min-max fairness as p tends to infinity. The goal is to minimize $\frac{1}{T}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} d(x_t, x_{t-1})\big) + g\big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} A_t x_t\big)$.

This setting raises several questions. First, how hard is the long-term fairness regularizer intrinsically? Online algorithms are commonly evaluated by their regret or by their competitive ratio against a dynamic offline benchmark which, unlike a static benchmark restricted to a single fixed action, can adapt its action sequence over time with full knowledge of the context. A finite competitive ratio is attainable for online optimization with switching costs, but whether any online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, even without switching costs, remains an open question; prior work has only conjectured that finite performance might be impossible in similar settings. Second, if such guarantees are out of reach, against what kind of benchmark can meaningful, practically relevant performance guarantees be established? Third, how can an online algorithm reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost and the long-term fairness cost with provable worst-case guarantees, when the per-round objective carries a memory of previous actions, and how does the long-term fairness regularizer affect such guarantees?

taches.questions:
Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

taches.questions:
Deep neural networks trained with first-order optimization methods have achieved remarkable empirical success across diverse domains. Despite their widespread adoption, a rigorous theoretical understanding of their optimization dynamics and generalization behavior remains incomplete, particularly for networks with ReLU activations. The difficulty stems from the non-smoothness and non-convexity of the loss landscape induced by ReLU activations and network architectures, which complicate classical analyses. Intriguingly, over-parameterized models often reach zero training error and still generalize well in the absence of explicit regularization, a phenomenon that has spurred substantial theoretical research into its underlying mechanisms.

A prominent line of research analyzes neural network training through the neural tangent kernel (NTK). In the infinite-width limit, the dynamics of gradient descent (GD) can be characterized by functions in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the NTK, and convergence guarantees have been established for both shallow and deep networks: provided the width is sufficiently large, GD converges to a global minimum within a neighborhood of its initialization. In this regime, generalization errors of order $L\sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/n}$ have been obtained for networks of depth $L$ trained on $n$ examples, where $\mathbf{H}^\infty$ denotes the NTK Gram matrix over the training data, but only for widths polynomial in $n$, $L$ and $1/\lambda_0$, with $\lambda_0$ the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{H}^\infty$. Requiring $\lambda_0>0$ is a strong assumption, because this eigenvalue tends to zero as the size of the training set grows. A weaker assumption is that the data are separable by the NTK features at initialization with a margin $\gamma$. Under this assumption, a logarithmic width suffices for two-layer ReLU networks, with a risk bound of order $1/(\gamma^2\sqrt{n})$ derived from Rademacher complexity; this width result relies on the 1-homogeneity of two-layer ReLU networks, a property that does not hold for deep networks. Extensions to deep ReLU networks yield bounds that still decay only as $1/\sqrt{n}$ and contain either factors exponential in depth, such as $4^L$, or additional width-dependent terms. A rate of order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ has so far been derived only for two-layer ReLU networks. More generally, uniform-convergence analyses based on Rademacher complexity or covering numbers can lead to vacuous bounds, typically depend exponentially on the depth, and usually yield rates of order $1/\sqrt{n}$.

A complementary line of research relies on algorithmic stability. Building on the observation that the spectral norm of the Hessian of wide networks scales with the width $m$ as $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{m})$, stability analyses have obtained bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$ for shallow networks, which is almost optimal in view of known lower bounds, and have been extended to deep networks with bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(e^{O(L)}/(n\gamma^2))$. These analyses, however, assume smooth activation functions and cannot be applied to non-smooth ReLU networks; for deep networks, they also incur an exponential dependence on depth, both in the bound and in the required width.

In summary, existing results either exhibit the suboptimal $1/\sqrt{n}$ dependence on the sample size, are restricted to shallow networks, require smooth activations, or depend exponentially on the depth $L$. A natural and fundamental question is therefore whether GD on deep ReLU networks can achieve generalization rates comparable to the minimax optimal rates established in the kernel setting, namely the SVM-type rate of order $1/(n\gamma^2)$. Specifically, for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$: Can risk bounds of the optimal order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ be established? Can the exponential dependence on the depth $L$ be replaced by a polynomial dependence $\mathrm{poly}(L)$? And how much over-parameterization (network width) do such guarantees require?

taches.questions:
Predicting the intermediate trajectories between an initial and a target distribution is a central problem in generative modeling. Tasks such as crowd navigation or modeling cell-state transitions under perturbation involve learning a transport map between two empirically observed endpoint distributions, rather than from the noisy prior required by denoising diffusion and flow matching. The Schrödinger bridge problem seeks an optimal stochastic map between a pair of endpoint distributions that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence to an underlying reference process. Schrödinger bridge matching solves this problem by learning a drift field that matches a mixture of conditional stochastic bridges between endpoint pairs, and generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations add a non-linear state cost, interpretable as the potential energy of the system, to describe systems whose optimal dynamics are not captured by the standard squared-Euclidean cost of entropic optimal transport.

These approaches have important limitations. They typically assume conservation of mass from the initial to the target distribution, which fails to capture dynamical population behaviors such as the growth and destruction of mass that are common in single-cell population data. They also model a single stochastic path: samples are transported from the initial distribution to the target through independent stochastic trajectories, without accounting for branching dynamics, so these methods are inherently limited to unimodal transitions and cannot capture branched or divergent evolution from a common origin to multiple distinct modes. When a system follows a branched trajectory that diverges toward several target modes, approximating the multi-modal target by simulating many independent particles is susceptible to mode collapse, with particles concentrating on dominant high-density modes or traversing only low-energy intermediate paths. Even when particles do reach several modes, counting where they end up gives only an indirect estimate of how mass splits across trajectories: it neither describes how mass is distributed over time nor reveals when the population begins to diverge toward different targets.

Yet branching is central to many real-world systems. When a homogeneous cell population undergoes a perturbation such as a gene knockout or a drug treatment, it frequently undergoes fate bifurcation, splitting into multiple phenotypically distinct outcomes or committing to divergent cell fates. Such trajectories are observable in single-cell RNA sequencing data, where each subpopulation evolves independently and grows or contracts along its trajectory toward a distinct terminal state. Predicting how cell states change after a perturbation is a crucial problem for therapeutic design, but the intermediate states between the unperturbed and perturbed populations are usually unknown, and intermediate snapshots are often sparse or unavailable. Related work leaves this gap open. Branched dynamics have been explored for optimal transport and Brownian motion, but matching one initial distribution to multiple terminal distributions through stochastic bridges has not been explicitly formulated; branching Brownian motion, for instance, describes particles that proliferate in number rather than a fixed population whose mass divides among distinct trajectories with their own terminal states. Some unbalanced transport methods that model growth rely on reconstruction losses on observed intermediate snapshots and fail to learn meaningful trajectories when these snapshots are unavailable, and existing models of perturbation responses either predict only the terminal perturbed state or model a single unimodal trajectory between one pair of boundary distributions.

This raises the following questions. Given samples from an initial population and from a terminal population that has split into several distinct modes, each holding a known share of the total mass, how can one learn a set of energy-minimizing stochastic bridges that represent the divergence of the population from a common origin into multiple distinct terminal states? How can such a model determine when and where branching occurs, and how mass is redistributed among branches over time, so that each terminal mode receives its observed share while trajectories follow low-energy paths under a task-specific state cost? And can such branched dynamics be recovered from initial and terminal snapshots alone, without intermediate-time supervision and without the mode collapse that affects single-path bridge matching?

taches.questions:
Graphs are powerful abstractions for representing complex relationships between entities, from social networks to molecular structures, and learning effective graph representations is crucial for node classification, graph classification and link prediction. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning, building representations through a message-passing mechanism that iteratively aggregates local neighborhood information. Despite its success, message passing faces several key limitations, such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. Numerous efforts address different aspects of these limitations: graph transformer architectures incorporate long-range interactions across broader graph contexts, positional encodings inject structural priors to improve global topological awareness, and graph rewiring techniques modify the topology to mitigate structural bottlenecks and enhance information diffusion.

However, these advances remain constrained by a cognitive discrepancy. Humans perceive global structure intuitively, following visual Gestalt principles: they understand the whole before analyzing the individual parts. GNNs and their variants, by contrast, operate through bottom-up processing. People instantly recognize ring structures, symmetric structures and critical bridges in a drawing of a graph, yet even advanced architectures struggle with such basic topological understanding: standard message-passing networks provably cannot identify bridges, and graphs that people tell apart at a glance can fool message passing unless sophisticated topological computations are added. Although architectural innovations have made significant theoretical and practical progress, their essence is still to identify and repair different aspects of the inherent defects of message passing. Approaches that perceive graphs visually remain largely unexplored for graph learning, despite their natural alignment with how humans perceive network structures, and despite a flourishing computer vision ecosystem whose models excel at holistic pattern recognition and global structure understanding. Recent work has begun to bring graph drawings into existing architectures, for instance into vision-language models for graph reasoning or into GNNs to enhance expressivity, but it treats graph layouts and vision models as black boxes, without examining how visual and message-passing models fundamentally differ in the way they understand graphs.

A second obstacle is measurement. Established benchmarks built from molecules, citation networks or protein interaction graphs tightly couple domain-specific node features with topology, which makes their separate contributions hard to quantify and can let models succeed through feature-based shortcuts rather than genuine structural understanding. Models that replace the true molecular topology with fixed-structure expander graphs have been shown to match or exceed performance on several molecular benchmarks, suggesting that node features often dominate structural information in standard datasets, potentially masking differences in how models perceive graph topology. The theoretical evaluation of GNNs has centered on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which measures the ability to distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs of the same size; valuable for theory, it is limited to binary discrimination between fixed-size graph pairs. Recent graph benchmarks oriented toward large language models focus on structural analysis tasks such as node counting, cycle detection and path finding, and typically rely on a limited set of random graph generators (such as Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) that inadequately capture topological diversity. What remains missing is a way to assess human-like graph cognition: the intuitive ability to perceive, abstract and reason about fundamental global graph properties, and to recognize the same connectivity patterns across varying scales and contexts.

This leads to the questions addressed here. Could models designed for visual perception, which carry no graph-specific inductive bias, offer a viable pathway to graph structural understanding, and do they process graph information in the same way as message-passing GNNs or through fundamentally different strategies? How can a model's ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties be evaluated rigorously, in isolation from domain-specific features, including whether it recognizes the same structural pattern regardless of graph size? And what does it take for a graph learning model to acquire the holistic, scale-robust understanding of topology that humans display effortlessly?

taches.questions:
Diffusion models, and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models in particular, have made astonishing progress in the quality of generated images. At the same time, emerging work on generative depth estimation has revealed that advanced T2I models hold a latent potential for depth estimation: the rich visual priors stored in a pre-trained T2I model can be leveraged to obtain strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation. Exploring a framework that bridges image generation and depth estimation is an essential step toward building unified models for both generation and visual perception.

Existing routes toward such unification each carry a substantial cost. The pioneering generative depth estimation paradigm repurposes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model by fine-tuning its denoising network with full parameters on depth data. It achieves powerful zero-shot depth estimation, but the parameter updates made during training irreversibly and catastrophically degrade the model's original image generation capability; later generative depth estimators that refine this recipe (for example with flow matching, geometry switchers or detail-preserving tuning strategies) inherit the same full-parameter fine-tuning and therefore the same loss. A second route unifies generation and depth estimation with a parallel dual-model architecture, in which two diffusion models run side by side and interact through feature-exchange operations; this requires running two diffusion models in parallel, and the interaction registers new knowledge into the pre-trained generator, which can affect its original image generation behaviour. A third, data-driven route trains a unified generation-and-perception model from scratch on massive multitask data (on the order of a hundred million samples). Despite remarkable progress, these solutions may be considered inefficient or resource-intensive, and potentially suboptimal.

Since a rich visual prior is already stored in advanced T2I models, a natural question arises: can a T2I model effortlessly acquire depth estimation capability without degrading its image generation capability? More concretely, starting from a fixed pre-trained T2I model, with a focus on modern transformer-based diffusion models, how can its latent depth estimation ability be unleashed so that a single model serves both image generation and depth estimation, keeping the original generation ability fully intact, adding only a small fraction of extra learnable parameters, and without resorting to massive multitask training data, while still reaching depth accuracy competitive with full-parameter fine-tuning and with existing unified models?

The problem is challenging. Among the effectively infinite pixel-level combinations that a T2I model learns to generate, there may exist underlying information highly correlated with scene depth; however, because text prompts provide only weak guidance and depth information is sparsely represented within the overall data distribution, extracting depth-relevant features from a fixed pre-trained T2I model is difficult. Any additional capacity must also make efficient use of the visual knowledge already present in the pre-trained model, so that depth estimation is obtained at a small parameter and data cost rather than by building and training a second large model.

taches.questions:
Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text yet remain prone to both intrinsic aleatoric ambiguity and epistemic gaps in their learned knowledge. The latter can lead to hallucinations—confident outputs that are factually incorrect. Quantifying these uncertainties is critical for building safe AI systems deployable in high-stakes applications. In free-form natural language generation tasks such as question answering, this is especially challenging, as lexically distinct responses can still be semantically equivalent: uncertainty has to be measured over meanings rather than over token sequences.

A standard way to do so defines a distribution over semantic clusters of responses, obtained by marginalizing over output sequences and approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The total predictive uncertainty over these clusters decomposes into an aleatoric part, the entropy over clusters (semantic entropy), which captures the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers, and an epistemic part, which reflects the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage. For a question such as "Name a way to measure the Hubble constant", several distinct but correct answers (for instance, the distance ladder or gravitational lensing time delays) reflect aleatoric uncertainty, whereas answers that contradict scientific facts or admit ignorance reveal gaps in the model's knowledge and signal that it should abstain.

Estimating these quantities often relies on drawing large IID sample sets, which often contain semantically redundant outputs and waste compute. Semantic entropy quantifies aleatoric uncertainty by clustering generated outputs into semantic equivalence classes, and mutual information computed via iterative prompting has been used to lower-bound certain forms of epistemic uncertainty; despite their conceptual appeal, both require extensive sampling to produce stable estimates, limiting their use in low-resource settings. Diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, on the other hand, do not account for semantics. A more recent method steers generation toward semantic diversity, but it relies on token substitutions and remains restricted to autoregressive models (ARMs). Moreover, diversity heuristics are commonly applied during sampling without correcting for the bias they introduce, even though the uncertainties of interest are defined under the model's own distribution.

Meanwhile, uncertainty estimation methods have focused on ARMs, whereas masked diffusion models (MDMs), which extend masked language modeling by learning iterative denoising schedules that progressively resolve masked spans, have recently emerged as strong alternatives. Despite achieving text quality on par with state-of-the-art ARMs, MDMs remain largely overlooked in the context of uncertainty quantification.

This leaves several questions open. How can stable estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty be obtained for free-form answers from a small, fixed budget of generations, so that the samples cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones? How can this be done while keeping the estimates faithful to the model's own predictive distribution? And can a single approach serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models?

taches.questions:
Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?
